scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Clean & Prep the House (Most Important First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, dining area, entrance). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and storage spaces. - **Launder bedding, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least dust them). - **Wash windows/mirrors** for a bright, welcoming look. - *Why?* A clean home feels sacred and ready for guests—it’s the foundation for decorations. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decorative Lights)** - **Place diyas** in key areas: - **Entrance** (mandatory for Diwali—use a small table or wall-mounted holder). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Dining area** (if space allows). - **Balcony/porch** (if you have one). - **Use LED string lights** for a modern touch (safe and energy-efficient). - **Marigold garlands** (traditional) or **fairy lights** (for a soft glow). - *Tip:* If short on time, focus on the **entrance and living room** first—they make the biggest impact. ### **3. Quick Decor Updates (Minimal Effort, Big Impact)** - **Hang rangoli** (even a simple design at the entrance or near diyas). - **Place small decorative items**: - **Diwali-themed candles** (scented ones add ambiance). - **Mini statues** (Ganesha, Lakshmi, or lotus motifs). - **Fresh flowers** (marigolds or jasmine for a natural touch). - **Swap out throw pillows/blankets** for festive colors (gold, red, or orange). ### **4. Final Touches (Last-Minute)** - **Set up a small altar** (if you observe puja) with diyas, flowers, and incense. - **Arrange snacks/drinks** in a pretty tray (for guests). - **Test all lights** (diyas, bulbs, etc.) to avoid last-minute issues. - **Spritz air fresheners** (sandalwood or rose-scented) for a fresh feel. ### **5. Day Before Diwali (Quick Checklist)** - **Replenish diyas** (if using oil-based ones). - **Charge phone/laptop** (for photos/videos). - **Set out guest seating** (if hosting). - **Prepare a welcome note** (on the door or entrance). --- ### **Time-Saving Tips:** ✅ **DIY shortcuts**: - Use **glow sticks** (cheap and safe) as temporary diyas. - **Paint rocks** with gold paint for instant decor. - **Buy pre-made rangoli stencils** or use chalk for quick designs. ✅ **Delegate**: - Ask a family member to handle **lighting** while you focus on **cleaning**. - If you have kids, let them help with **hanging garlands or placing small diyas**. ✅ **Skip perfection**: - A few well-placed diyas + a clean entrance look **far more festive** than half-decorated rooms. --- ### **Sample Timeline (If You’re Short on Time):** - **Day 1 (Today)**: Clean + place diyas in entrance/living room. - **Day 2**: Add rangoli, garlands, and small decor items. - **Day 3 (Before Diwali)**: Final touches (lights, snacks, altar). --- **Most important priority?** **Cleanliness + entrance diyas**—they set the tone for guests. The rest can be layered in gradually. Wishing you a joyful Diwali! 🪔✨

If you’d stuck to *"I just don’t want white"* or *"colored dresses feel better to me,"* you could’ve avoided the meltdown. **Oversharing the deeper reason** (even if true) was a **misstep**—it made the conversation about *her* failure, not your choice. - **But here’s the twist**: If your mother **insisted on knowing the "real reason"** (which she had no right to demand), your honesty about the emotional tie-in was **raw but not inherently wrong**—it was the **delivery** that failed. She reacted poorly, but that doesn’t excuse your **brutal phrasing** ("I’m not innocent"). - **The apology gap**: - You’re **right** that she **pushed you into a corner** with repeated questions, but **you also had options**: - *"I don’t want to discuss this further. It’s my choice, and I’d prefer we focus on planning."* (Firm but kind.) - *"I’m not comfortable explaining further, but I promise we’ll find a dress you love."* (Boundaries + reassurance.) - Instead, you **let her dig until you cracked**, which escalated the conflict. **Apologizing now** isn’t just about fixing the moment—it’s about **acknowledging that your words hurt her**, even if her reactions were overblown. --- ### **2. Was it AITA? (Relational Perspective)** **Score: ~0.5/1** *(A mix of valid boundaries and poor conflict management.)* **Why?** - **You asserted your autonomy**, which is **healthy**—you’re not a child, and your wedding should reflect *your* values, not societal norms or her expectations. - **But you failed to navigate the emotional landmine**: - Your mother’s divorce is **her trauma**, not your dress choice. By tying your rejection of white to it, you **reopened a wound** without considering how it would land. **She wasn’t asking for a lecture on marriage statistics; she was asking for a dress.** - **Family dynamics are fragile**. Even if your reasoning was "logical," **emotions trump logic in these conversations**. Her reaction wasn’t about the dress—it was about **feeling dismissed and judged** by her daughter. - **The "only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiancé" stance**: - **Partially true**, but **not always practically possible**. In a family wedding, **some compromise or emotional labor is expected**—even if you don’t *want* to engage. Your mother’s excitement was **genuine**, and shutting her down entirely (even if justified) **hurts her feelings** and risks damaging your relationship. --- ### **3. The Core Issue: Why This Feels So Wrong (To You)** You’re **furious** because: 1. **You felt disrespected**—she was **pushing your boundaries** with repeated questions. 2. **You felt judged**—she implied your choice was "childish" or "unreasonable." 3. **You felt like she was controlling you**—even though *you* were the one setting the rule ("no white"). **But here’s the rub**: **Your anger is valid, but your mother’s feelings are also valid.** You can’t **only** prioritize your comfort in this exchange. **Family relationships require mutual respect**, even when you disagree. --- ### **How to Move Forward (If You Want to Repair)** 1. **Apologize sincerely** (even if you feel she overreacted): > *"Mom, I realize now that I handled this badly. I shouldn’t have said what I did about innocence, and I shouldn’t have made you feel like you had to justify your past. I love you, and I’m sorry I hurt your feelings. Let’s focus on finding a dress you’ll love—together."* - **Why this works**: It **acknowledges her feelings** without agreeing with her logic. It **closes the door** on the argument while **reaffirming your bond**. 2. **Redirect the conversation**: - If she brings up the divorce again, **gently steer back to the dress**: > *"I know this is hard for you, and I’m sorry. But let’s talk about colors you love—maybe we can find something that feels special to both of us."* 3. **Set boundaries for the future**: - If she **keeps pressuring you**, you can say: > *"I’ve made my choice, and I’d love it if we could respect that. I’m happy to discuss the dress, but not why I picked it."* 4. **Consider a compromise**: - If you **really** want to honor her, you could: - Pick a **non-traditional white alternative** (e.g., ivory, blush, or a white dress with **bold accents** in a color she loves). - Let her **help you pick the accessories** (veil, shoes, jewelry) where she can feel involved. --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It AITA?** **Technically: Yes (but not maliciously).** - You **had the right to choose a colored dress**, but **how you communicated it was cruel and unnecessary**. - You **didn’t need to reveal the divorce connection**, and **your phrasing was harsh**. - **Her reaction was over-the-top**, but **your response was also over-the-top in the other direction** (dismissive + defensive). **The bigger issue**: **You both failed to meet each other halfway.** - She **didn’t respect your autonomy** by pushing for answers. - You **didn’t respect her feelings** by shutting her down and revealing painful personal ties. --- ### **What You Can Learn** 1. **Family conversations about personal choices are emotional mines**. **Softening your approach** (e.g., *"I don’t want white, but I’d love your help picking something else"*) could’ve avoided the meltdown. 2. **You don’t owe anyone an explanation**—but **how you say "no" matters**. A simple *"I’ve decided, and I’d appreciate your support"* would’ve been stronger than escalating. 3. **Apologizing isn’t about being wrong—it’s about repairing**. Even if you feel she overreacted, **her feelings were real**, and dismissing them (even indirectly) **hurts**. --- ### **Would I Give You a 0 or 1?** **0.3/1** (Not a full "1" because your choice was valid, but the **execution was flawed**). **But here’s the thing**: **This isn’t about a score—it’s about growth.** - If you **apologize sincerely** and **move forward with kindness**, this can **strengthen your relationship**. - If you **double down on defensiveness**, it’ll **fester into resentment**. **You’re allowed to be stubborn about your dress.** But **love requires more than just being right—it requires grace.** Would you like help drafting a more diplomatic way to handle similar conversations in the future?
